title: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Indeed, by looking at such slices one can readily identify the very same four classes of behavior as in one-dimensional cellular automata.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 6, “Starting from Randomness”; section “Four Classes of Behavior” (from p. 231), p. 245. Scope: two-dimensional cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch06-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing software and pattern catalogs support broad tests and directly establish examples such as Life. They cannot validate an exhaustive taxonomy over the unrestricted two-dimensional rule universe.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample defined families of two-dimensional rules, evolve random and sparse initial states, and classify one-dimensional time slices using preregistered order, entropy, periodicity, and localized-structure criteria. Test whether the resulting behaviors exhaust four categories and include robust class 4 examples.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Class boundaries are informal.

Sampling all two-dimensional rule spaces is impossible.

Slice-based classes may omit genuinely two-dimensional organization.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.54
discriminating power: 0.68
data existence: 0.94
analysis feasibility: 0.84

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The 5-neighbor totalistic rules that preserve a white background are a small finite list, and Life is simulated and censused in public software, so the slice comparison and the white-background clause are practical. The sentence says two-dimensional cellular automata in general show the same four classes, which that list does not cover. Slices are a useful proxy and also a possible confound.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Evolve the small two-dimensional totalistic rules and the Game of Life from random and near-blank seeds, then classify one-dimensional slices by the same activity and damage criteria used in one dimension. Failure of those slices to use all four types, or failure of Life to sustain localized objects on a white background, would challenge the corresponding clause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Life is much better archived than the general two-dimensional claim.

Small totalistic codes do not exhaust two-dimensional rules.

A one-dimensional slice can display a class the full two-dimensional field does not.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.64
discriminating power: 0.62
